extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent prosecutors, and examiners (software/computer-related inventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting claims and specifications (and prosecuting applications) to survive 35 U.S.C. § 101 subject-matter eligibility challenges for computer-implemented and related technologies. Emphasizes showing technical problems/solutions, technical improvements, and specification support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical problem/technical solution emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Include description of technical problem/solution, focusing on making sure the problem is portrayed as a technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice tip: The specification bolsters eligibility when it explains the technological problem being solved (e.g., network vulnerabilities) and describes the technological solution. Quote/recite technical harms or network-specific issues in the spec to show the claims are rooted in computer technology rather than abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite technical limitations improving computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be directed to improvements in existing computer functionality (e.g., improving functioning of computer systems, networks, GUIs, memory architectures) rather than mere abstract ideas or generic computer use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-oriented key manager and label use that improve network security (TecSec); plurality of network monitors that analyze specific types of data and integrate reports to identify intruders (SRI); specific graphical user interface structures that improve speed, accuracy, and usability (Trading Techs). Cast the invention as 'an improvement to the capability of the system as a whole.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Support improvements with specification details and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specification-level technical details and explain benefits that flow from the claimed improvement (how and why the improvement works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If drafting, include and explain benefits and technical details in the specification; if in prosecution, try to identify and emphasize specifics in the record to 'hang your hat on.' Courts look to the specification to decide whether claims are directed to a technological improvement (Visual Memory; Univ. of Florida).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claims that are merely human cognitive actions or mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not draft method claims whose steps can be performed as human cognitive actions or otherwise amount to mental processes or fundamental human activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit treats claims drawn to activities like voting/verifying as abstract if they correspond to longstanding human activities (Voter Verified). To avoid this, include steps or limitations that cannot be performed purely mentally and/or are tied to specific technical implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft system claims that do not merely mirror method claims and include non-standard components
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, include system claims with components that are not simply 'standard components' and that are supported in the specification as being specially configured or non-generic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice tip: system claims that merely restate method steps with generic computers/printers/etc. are insufficient (Voter Verified). Include and support in the spec components that can be shown to be more than standard off-the-shelf hardware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the prior-art problem as technological and claim a specific technological solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Cast the problem in the prior art in terms of technology and ensure claims recite a specific implementation that solves that technological problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit favored claims that addressed specific technology problems (e.g., prior GUI deficiencies) and recited specific structured solutions. Emphasize lack of pre-electronic analog or that solution is specific to software/computer context (Trading Techs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific structured claim elements (not just 'displaying' or generic data handling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that require a specific, structured element paired with prescribed functionality (e.g., a structured GUI with fixed axes and moving indicators) are more likely to avoid abstraction than claims that merely claim displaying or manipulating data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claims recite structure and specific interaction between structure and function, rather than high-level data presentation. Show how the structure resolves identified prior-art problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide technical explanation of functional elements (avoid purely functional language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on bare functional recitations (e.g., 'drivers' or other elements described only functionally) without explaining how those elements operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court criticized claims where drivers or other elements were recited only functionally without detail. If operation of elements is explained in the specification, it may help eligibility (Univ. of Florida).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show an inventive concept at Alice/Mayo step two via technical modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is characterized as invoking an abstract idea at step one, demonstrate at step two that the claim includes an inventive concept—technical modifications or improvements beyond well-understood, routine, conventional components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the static price index constituting an inventive concept in a trading system context (Trading Techs). Merely citing standard components (PC, display, keyboard, printer) is not enough to transform an abstract claim into eligible subject matter (Voter Verified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere automation of conventional practices ('do it on a computer')
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely implement conventional pen-and-paper or business practices on a generic computer are likely ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat simple automation without technical detail as insufficient. Demonstrate how the claimed invention effects a technical change or provides a technical solution, not just faster/better business processing (Univ. of Florida; Voit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize technical distinctions over the prior art in both claims and specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the specification and claims highlight any technical distinctions over prior art and that such distinctions are reflected in claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice guidance: focus on ensuring the specification describes a technical distinction over the prior art that is reflected in the claims (TecSec). Use the specification to show how claimed features differ and improve over known technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitation of multiple, specific categories/limitations can strengthen technical character
rubrics_metrics.description: Listing multiple specific categories, data types, or categories of monitored data in the claim may help demonstrate a technical solution rather than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: SRI's claim listed multiple categories of network traffic data and an integration step; the recitation of multiple categories and integration may have supported eligibility. Consider including concrete categories and how they are processed.

rubrics_metrics.name: When dealing with user-interface inventions emphasize improved functionality unique to the UI
rubrics_metrics.description: For GUI-related inventions, claim the specific UI structure and functionality that directly solve prior UI problems (speed, accuracy, usability) rather than claiming generic UI actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the UI has no pre-electronic analog and that the claimed structure imparts functionality to the system as a whole. Use concrete UI structure+behavior to demonstrate technical improvement (Trading Techs; IBG/Liu guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: In prosecution, identify and emphasize any existing technical detail to rely on
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application text is already drafted, during prosecution try to find underemphasized technical features or details that can be used to defend eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tip: look in the specification for technical details, examples, or performance/benefit language to emphasize to the examiner or in litigation as evidence of a technological improvement (Visual Memory; Univ. of Florida).
